blocks.heading: The *touch-through* yet deep analysis of all that has gone often brings us to a moment — a moment that *reflects the past* and at times defines it to be the *pivot* of a lifetime.

blocks.leftColumn: *Ram stands at such a moment.* He puts forward the first step towards the war — a step from land to water —
blocks.rightColumn: and recalls everything that has brought him here, keeping himself as a part of his own inception.

blocks.heading: Thinking about all that has brought him to this point — when he is just about to step into the ocean — Close to his heart lies Seeta, who at this very moment is in Ashoka Vatika, surrounded by the unknowns, the demons.Ravana, the learned Brahmin, the greatest devotee of Shiva, must be worshipping — in his quest to win the war.
Ram remembers how it all started. With Sita’s swayamvara. He did not just lift the divine bow and string it — which was the challenge — he broke it. A fracture that began a chain of destiny.

blocks.leftColumn: *He is about to step into the ocean, where the team of Nala and Neer are  constructing a divine floating bridge for their master — the prince of Ayodhya.*
blocks.rightColumn:
He looks at the floating stones and recalls — How Lakshmana cut off the nose and left ear of शूपर्णखा Shurpanakha, Ravana’s sister, who was smitten by the beauty and youth of both brothers.

How he crossed that first trap — yet eventually they were drawn into the greater one — the illusion of Maarich<ref n="01"/>,the golden deer.

annotations.text:
Not temptation through desire, but through wonder.
Maarich became the perfect distraction — beautiful enough to be pursued, unreal enough to conceal danger. In the Ramayana, illusion rarely arrives as fear; it arrives as fascination.

blocks.leftColumn: जटायू Jaṭāyū — a divine bird, younger son of Aruṇa. His brother, Sampati, a demi-god in the form of a vulture, an old friend of Dasharatha. Jatayu fought valiantly with Ravana while he was flying Seeta towards Lanka on the Pushpak Vimana.
blocks.rightColumn: The calm of birds still remains with Ram — adding dimension to his attack, forming his silent Air Force.

blocks.heading: Physically, Ram looks around. He looks across. But in his mind, he looks back — at everything that has brought him to this great war. The war — perhaps the greatest reason for his incarnation.

In each version I paint, I see the story in a different shade of the same color. I believe that questioning relates to a greater mind—one that works for the collective good. These doubts are divinely inspired and inform every render.

blocks.leftColumn: In one version, I imagine him questioning his violence toward Shurpanakha; in another, he reflects on whether breaking Shiva’s bow was wrong. He might also question his willingness to believe in a golden deer after surviving in the jungle for nearly 14 years. Ultimately, he concludes that while Ravana’s kidnapping of Sita was wrong, the manner in which it was done was a far graver offense.
blocks.rightColumn: By disguising himself as a sadhu, <ref n="02"/> Ravana’s action became a dangerous template for ages to follow—where a perceived saint is a demon within. This is not just a wrong committed against one person, but an affront to society as a whole, inspiring a world where the guise of goodness is used to hide the intent to do harm.

annotations.text: Inspired by a conversation between Shiva & Parvati, mentioned in Shiv Puraan.
